subject: fitting multiple sets of data with same model

messages.author: e1c430550f86b1f6
messages.subject: fitting multiple sets of data with same model
parts:
HI all,

I am using STAN from R.

And, this seems to trivial question, but just want to be sure:

I have K of the following data set:

y [1... N]
x [1... N]

that I would like to fit into a simple linear mode for each set:

y ~ normal (beta * x, sigma)


Does it make any difference (if so, what are the pros/cons) if I
a) run each of the K linear regression separately by calling the sampling function for each set (such that in the parameter block, there  would have only 1-pair of beta and simga)
b) load all K data sets and have STAN fits all of them in 1 go (such that in the parameter block, there  would have K-pairs of beta and simga)

More generally, from R, if i want to run a bunch of regressions, would it better to run each of them separately or collect all data and send them to STAN in 1 go?

Many thanks,
Andy

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] fitting multiple sets of data with same model
parts:
I'm going to try to clarify the question first. Suppose
your data looks like this:

vector[N] y[K];
vector[N] x[K];

and parameters you want to estimate are:

real beta[K];
real sigma[K];

You should get the same posterior for each beta[k]
and sigma[k] if you have a single Stan program with
likelihood:

for (k in 1:K) {
y[k] ~ normal(beta[k] * x[k], sigma[k]);
beta[k] ~ ... some prior ...
sigma[k] ~ .. some prior ...
}

or if you run K separate instances of Stan with
likelihood

y[k] ~ normal(beta[k] * x[k], sigma[k];
beta[k] ~ ... some prior ...
sigma[k] ~ .. some prior ...

Now if you provide a hierarchical prior things will be
different, which I'd strongly advise if the K instances
are exchangeable.

- Bob

messages.author: df2011c04ce6269d
messages.subject: Re: fitting multiple sets of data with same model
parts:
What you're asking is whether mixturing datasets would cause any difference.
refer to this: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixture_distribution
in your case, all weight of mixture are identical as (1/K).
If you're sure that all datasets follow identical distributions and are independent to each other, in other words, they're come from the same source and that source is memoryless about longer past, then mixing them won't cause any difference. This can be proved directly by mixture's defination.

Markov Chain Monte Carlo also comes with Markov property which mean it's memoryless. In other words, a sampled parameters generally won't cause the whole chains' distribution different

On Thursday, March 19, 2015 at 2:16:51 AM UTC-4, andy...@cubist-asia.com wrote:
hi guys,

Many thanks.

Yes, my original question was more about parallel development as I'm trying to get my arms around development with STAN/rstan in terms of how to split the codes across the 2 layers.

Do as much outside of Stan itself as possible---the reason is you'll need it in R anyway for flexible model checking anyway and while Stan is quite flexible in its transformed data block
it's not as easy to trouble shoot as R (though amazing compared to BUGS).  If you do anything in the parameters/transformed parameter/model block that could be instead done in R (or the
transformed data block) you're wasting CPU time as it gets done once per leapfrog step (many times per iteration).  If your model goes fast anyway this isn't as much of an issue as the model
checking aspect.  Krzysztof

It is also correct that the different K components don't necessarily come from the same source.

Cheers,

Andy

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: fitting multiple sets of data with same model
parts:
> On Mar 20, 2015, at 1:19 AM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Thursday, March 19, 2015 at 2:16:51 AM UTC-4, andy...@cubist-asia.com wrote:
> hi guys,
>
> Many thanks.
>
> Yes, my original question was more about parallel development as I'm trying to get my arms around development with STAN/rstan in terms of how to split the codes across the 2 layers.
>
> Do as much outside of Stan itself as possible---the reason is you'll need it in R anyway for flexible model checking anyway and while Stan is quite flexible in its transformed data block
> it's not as easy to trouble shoot as R (though amazing compared to BUGS). If you do anything in the parameters/transformed parameter/model block that could be instead done in R (or the
> transformed data block) you're wasting CPU time as it gets done once per leapfrog step (many times per iteration).

The number of times the transformed parameters and model blocks
get executed is upper bounded by 2^(treedepth + 1), but it's usually
exactly 2^treedepth. CmdStan actually dumps out the number of leapfrog
steps now, I believe.

But the real killer is that any variables introduced in the model
block or transformed parameters block go on the autodiff stack,
which makes taking gradients slower, and that's the real bottleneck.

Anything that can be moved from transformed parameters to either

* transformed data: operates on doubles, once per chain

* generated quantities: operates on doubles, once per iteration

is a big win. I'm guessing using our generated quantities would
save CPU time vs. R, but the problem is that it gets written into the
output file, which sucks up memory if you're running through R or
I/O if you run through CmdStan.

- Bob
